title: Property Search
excerpt: How to run a land search — online via ArdhiSasa or manually with Form LRA 84 — what it reveals about ownership and encumbrances, plus how to do a historical (Ndung'u) search.
content:
There are a variety of searches to be conducted, but the modern conveyancer is more concerned with a search at the Land Registry, Company Registry, Survey Department, and so on.

The search should be conducted at the relevant land registry countrywide — i.e. the registry where the property is located.

What a land-office search looks for

  • Issues regarding ownership.
  • Issues regarding tenure / interest in the property.
  • Special conditions imposed on the property, especially a leasehold.
  • The permitted user — whether commercial, residential, etc.
  • The existence of any adverse entries, e.g. restrictions (the property is under investigation), cautions (placed by someone claiming a right in the property), inhibitions and charging orders (an ongoing court process), and a charge (the property is held as collateral for a loan).
  • The name of the registered owner, the land number, the size, and the owner's address.

How to search for a property

The search can be virtual or manual.

Online search through ArdhiSasa

  1. Create an ArdhiSasa account: enter your National ID number and KRA PIN on the portal (ardhisasa.lands.go.ke), then verify via phone or email.
  2. Upload the required documents and input the title deed number for the property.
  3. Pay the prescribed KES 1,000 search fee via bank transfer, debit/credit card, or M-Pesa.
  4. The registered landowner must approve the search request within ArdhiSasa before it can be processed.
  5. Track the status on your dashboard — the digital Land Search Certificate is typically available within one to three days.

Manual search

To search manually, you will need:

  • A copy of the land title deed.
  • A copy of your national ID.
  • A copy of your KRA PIN certificate.
  • A service charge fee of KES 1,000.
  • An application for search, Form LRA 84.

Where to begin:

  1. Fill Form LRA 84 in triplicate.
  2. Attach copies of the title deed, your ID, and your KRA PIN certificate.
  3. Pay the KES 1,000 fee at the lands registry and keep your receipt.
  4. Present the search form — the registrar inspects the register.
  5. Return after five working days to collect the results.

What the search document reveals

  • Name and address of the registered landowner.
  • Size of the land and type of ownership (freehold or leasehold).
  • Encumbrances or conditions limiting free use of the land — court orders, loans (where the land is security), and cautions, if any.
  • Title and search numbers.
  • Date of the land search.

The certificate of official search (Form LRA 85) must be signed and sealed by the Lands Registrar, the custodian of the documents in the lands office.

What is a historical search?

This has been prompted in modern conveyancing by the Ndung'u Report of 2004 into the Illegal Allocation of Land. To access the correspondence file you write a letter to the Land Registry and access is granted. Correspondence arises from the history of the land — when it was registered, subdivided, and so on.

You may carry out a historical search on land allotted via the general file (zone file, correspondence file, etc.). When searching on the basis of a letter of allotment, look out for planning by the local authority, and for the Part Development File (PDF), which should be properly prepared and signed by the Chief Physical Planner and the Commissioner of Lands.

Other searches

  • Companies registry — reveals whether a corporate seller still exists, any insolvency proceedings, its legal standing, authority to sell, and who may execute conveyancing instruments.
  • Survey department — confirms the boundaries; they must be recognisable and clearly definable.
  • County government — discloses zoning/development policy and any adverse proposals, e.g. compulsory acquisition for public purposes.
  • Court registry — discloses any ongoing proceedings regarding the property.
  • Physical site visit — confirms location, access roads, and existing developments.

title: Investigation of Title
excerpt: Why a buyer must investigate title even after signing — searching the register, making pre-contract enquiries, and inspecting the title document for proper execution, stamp duty, and hidden encumbrances.
content:
The surge of forgeries and fraud involving title documents means a purchaser must investigate the title even after the contract is executed, to establish that the document of title was acquired through a proper and lawful process.

Investigation is not confined to the registry or the title deed alone — it also extends to the physical property. Conveyancing practice allows parties to investigate even after the contract is executed, through the methods below.

Methods of investigating title

Search on the title

Inspection of the title or register records at the relevant lands registry, to detect any adverse (unfavourable) entry on the title or the register itself.

Pre-contract (preliminary) enquiries

Enquiries to the seller seeking information not covered by the searches, including matters touching the physical state of the property. The seller is under no duty to reply, but if they do, the reply must be accurate — one you can rely on. Ask about:

  • The tenants or occupants and the terms of their occupation or tenancy.
  • Any physical defect the vendor is aware of but which inspection does not easily reveal.
  • The development prospects of neighbouring properties.
  • Whether there have been any boundary changes in the last few years.

Inspection of the title document

Things to look out for:

  • Whether the document was properly executed and witnessed — e.g. for a company, the common seal affixed in the presence of two directors, and a proper power of attorney where used.
  • Whether the correct stamp duty was paid.
  • Whether any encumbrances or adverse interests are noted on the title, e.g. special conditions or limitations.

title: The Green Card (and White Card)
excerpt: The Green Card is the registry's authoritative ownership-history record for freehold land. Here's how it relates to the mother title, the White Card for leaseholds, and how to obtain a certified copy.
content:
The Green Card is an official record maintained by the lands registry detailing all transactions and the ownership history of freehold land. When a subdivision is done, a Green Card is opened for each resulting parcel — a new title must be preceded by opening a card for it, and any subsequent transactions are recorded there.

When land is sold or subdivided, the mother title remains at the registry, where it is cancelled and rendered incapable of supporting further transactions. New titles are then issued to reflect the subdivisions. Likewise, the Green Card for the mother title is closed, and separate Green Cards are opened for the newly created parcels.

Because the new titles must correspond with the entries on the Green Card, they usually retain a reference to the mother title number. The Green Card also helps confirm the authenticity of a title deed: while title documents can be forged, the information on the Green Card is regarded as more authoritative. A purchaser, through an advocate, can apply for a certified copy of the closed Green Card to trace the root of title.

Considerations for the Green Card

  • As a reference document, its information must match the information on any document relating to the property.
  • Any activity affecting ownership is entered on the Green Card.
  • When land is subdivided, a new Green Card is opened for each subdivided plot.
  • A Green Card is held at the land registry.

How to request a typed or certified copy

  • Access is generally limited to authorised persons — advocates, surveyors, or the registered proprietor.
  • Submit a written application at the relevant land registry.
  • Provide the land details (title number and location).
  • Pay the applicable search fee and obtain an official receipt (some registries charge an additional processing fee).
  • Return after five working days for a certified copy, typed copy, or extract of the Green Card.

After obtaining the Green Card, compare its particulars with those on the title deed. Any discrepancy may suggest forgery or ownership irregularities — it is advisable to seek professional assistance when verifying land documentation.

The White Card (for leaseholds)

Leasehold titles use a White Card — the register of the leasehold proprietor and the key document verifying ownership of leasehold land in Kenya. It is essentially the leasehold equivalent of the Green Card, containing the full history of the lease: from the original allotment and lease instrument to subsequent transfers, charges, and conditions.

How to apply for a copy of the White Card

  1. Prepare an application letter addressed to the County Land Registrar (if registered locally) or the Chief Land Registrar (if centrally registered), including your full details and contact information, the parcel number and location, and the purpose of the request; attach copies of the title or lease documents and your identification (ID, passport, or company registration documents).
  2. Submit the letter and supporting documents to the relevant registry.
  3. Pay the required processing fee before the application is processed.
  4. The registry prepares the White Card (if not already opened) or issues a certified copy.
  5. Collect it by following up with your payment receipt — processing takes a few days to a few weeks; you may be asked to produce the original certificate of lease for verification.

title: Rights of Spouses to Land
excerpt: How a spouse acquires an interest in land, the mandatory spousal-consent rule for sales and charges since 2012, and how to register as a spouse to protect that interest.
content:
A spouse acquires an interest in their spouse's land if they contribute — by labour or other means — to the productivity, upkeep, and improvement of the land. Under the Land Registration Act, marriage includes a civil, customary, or religious marriage, and the spousal interest is recognised as if it were registered against the title.

Under Article 45(3) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, spouses have equal rights at the time of marriage, during the marriage, and at its dissolution. Note: in relation to land transactions this equality is interpreted strictly in regard to obtaining consent — spouses hold a beneficial interest in matrimonial property, but it does not mean an automatic 50–50 split.

The principle of equity is paramount: fairness is determined not by the quantum of each spouse's contribution but by the significance of any contribution — direct or indirect — that facilitates the acquisition of the property.

Section 14 of the Matrimonial Property Act provides two rebuttable presumptions for property acquired during a marriage: (a) that property held in the name of one spouse is held in trust for the other; and (b) that beneficial interests are equal where the property is in the spouses' joint names.

Spousal consent when disposing of land

Prior to 2012, under the Registered Land Act, spousal consent before disposing of land was not required. Since the Land Registration Act came into force in 2012, spousal consent is mandatory.

  • A purchaser has a duty to inquire whether the spouse has consented to the sale.
  • If consent was not obtained and the non-consenting spouse challenges the sale, the transfer to the purchaser is void.
  • No timeframe is specified within which a non-consenting spouse may bring such a challenge.
  • If the vendor's spouse refuses consent, the vendor cannot sell the property.
  • This extends to all land and is not limited to matrimonial property.

Spousal consent when charging property

The consent of the spouse(s) must be obtained before charging the land (using it as collateral to secure a loan). Likewise, before disposing of matrimonial property on default under a statutory power of sale, the spouse(s) must be served with a notice of sale in line with section 96(3) of the Land Registration Act.

Registering as a spouse

This is the process where a married person applies to be registered as the wife or husband of the person who owns the land.

What you will need

  • A copy of the land title deed.
  • A copy of your ID.
  • A copy of your KRA PIN certificate.
  • A fee assessed by the lands registry.
  • A copy of your marriage certificate.
  • The application form LRA 10.

Where to begin

  1. Fill Form LRA 10, stating the dates of the supporting documents.
  2. Support the request with a sworn statutory declaration, stamped by an Advocate or a Magistrate.
  3. Attach a copy of your ID and KRA PIN certificate.
  4. Pay the assessed fee at the lands registry and keep your receipt.
  5. Present the form at the registry for registration.

Result of the application

On receiving your application, the Registrar sends a notice to the person you say you are married to, informing them and asking whether they oppose it. They have 30 working days to oppose. If they do not, the Registrar registers you as a spouse within 10 working days.

Once registered, you are better placed to protect your rights by giving or refusing consent to dealings such as the sale, charge, or lease of the land by your husband or wife. Note: the registered proprietor may also apply to have their spouse's name included in the register.

title: Methods of Acquiring Title (and Cancellation of Title Deeds)
excerpt: The types of title deeds and how Kenyan law consolidated them, the six methods of acquiring title to land, and the grounds on which a title can be impeached or cancelled.
content:
A title deed is a document giving evidence of one's right to land. Different types of title deed existed under the various land Acts in force from colonial times through the post-independence era.

Types of title deed

  • Indenture — a title under the Government Lands Act, Cap 280 (repealed).
  • Grant — a government grant under the Registration of Titles Act, Cap 281 (repealed), and a county council grant under the Trust Land Act, Cap 288.
  • Certificate of title — a grant issued as a result of subdivision without change of user.
  • Certificate of lease — a title under the Registered Land Act, Cap 300 (repealed), for leasehold land.
  • Absolute title deed — a title under the Registered Land Act, Cap 300 (repealed), for freehold land.
  • Sectional title — a title for a unit within a building, such as a flat or apartment.

The Land Registration Act, 2012 consolidates these into the Certificate of Title (issued for freehold land) or the Certificate of Lease (for leasehold land).

Leasehold versus freehold

Leasehold is a form of land tenure where a lessee holds rights to land for a specific period and subject to conditions imposed by the lessor. The 999-year leases were all converted to 99-year leases with effect from 1 September 2009, when the current Constitution was promulgated.

Freehold is a form of tenure in which the owner has the maximum rights to land, without restriction as to the period of ownership or the rights exercisable on the land.

Methods of acquiring title to land

  • Allocation of public land — public land transferred by the government to individuals, usually on a leasehold basis, for a specified period and subject to conditions.
  • Land adjudication — determining and recording the rights and interests of individuals on community/trust land to facilitate registration of title.
  • Prescription / adverse possession — acquiring title by occupying land without opposition for a period of 12 years.
  • Settlement programmes — the government providing access to land for squatters or persons displaced by floods, development projects, conservation, or conflict.
  • Transmissions — ownership passing to another party where the owner's powers are restricted, as on death, bankruptcy, or liquidation of a company.
  • Transfers — the transfer of rights to land from one entity to another.

Cancellation of a title deed

Protection of a title can be removed and the title impeached where it was procured through fraud or misrepresentation to which the holder is proved to be a party, or where it was procured illegally, unprocedurally, or through a corrupt scheme.

  • Section 26 of the Land Registration Act, 2012 removes protection from an innocent purchaser or title holder — their title is impeachable — thereby protecting the true title holders from being deprived of their land by subsequent transactions.
  • Section 60 gives the Registrar power to rectify titles where there were wrongful or fraudulent entries.
  • Section 64 gives power to cancel a title when directed by a court.

title: Purchase of Land Through Shares in a Co-operative
excerpt: How to safely buy land by acquiring shares in a co-operative society or land-buying company — verifying the society's title, doing due diligence, and securing your share certificate and plot.
content:
Co-operative societies can own land, and the ownership is a tenancy in common. Members own shares in a company or society that owns the land — for example, parastatals, land-buying companies, and housing co-operatives. The key matters are how the purchaser comes to own shares, the land and acreage involved, and when subdivisions will take place.

The society must be the registered owner of the land, or must show an unbroken chain of documents leading to the root of title. An acquisition between the society and the purchaser must be signed, after which share or plot certificates are issued to members as proof of ownership. The share certificate should state the shares owned by the purchaser; by owning shares in the society, the purchaser owns a share in the land in common with the other shareholders.

How to protect your interests as a purchaser

  • Conduct a property search to confirm the society has a clean, unencumbered title — the mother title registered in the company's name, with documents demonstrating that ownership is legal, formal, and free from encumbrances.
  • Conduct due diligence on the affairs of the society and company — tax issues, ongoing litigation, management disputes, shareholder complaints, criminal investigations, overvaluation of the land, or overcharging of advocate's/surveyor's fees.
  • Keep your paperwork — a formal agreement, original receipts and acknowledgements of payment, your share certificate, and the ballot, to demonstrate you are a shareholder and confirm the sale.
  • Obtain a copy or extract of the original register containing the shareholders' names and plot numbers, and ensure it has an entry corresponding to your plot or reflects you as the owner.
  • Take physical possession of your apportioned parcel immediately, to avoid double allocations, encroachment, boundary disputes, adverse possession, or squatters.

title: Conveyancing & Taxation
excerpt: The taxes and duties in a Kenyan land transaction — stamp duty, capital gains tax, land rates, and land rent — including who pays, the rates, the exemptions, and how to pay.
content:
Stamp duty

Stamp duty is a duty levied on the legal recognition of certain documents. Every instrument relating to property in Kenya for which the Schedule to the Stamp Duty Act provides is assessed, and the required duty must be paid as a legal requirement. No document is accepted for registration unless the duty has been properly paid. The amount is set by the Minister of Finance and is usually stated in the Budget.

On a transfer, duty is assessed on the value of the property (ad valorem):

  • Within municipalities and cities (urban land) — 4%.
  • Outside municipalities and cities (agricultural land) — 2%.
  • Leases — based on the annual rent for which the property is leased.
  • Mortgages — 0.2% of the amount borrowed.
  • Discharges/charges — 0.05% of the amount borrowed.

Valuation is done by an independent government valuer. Duty must be paid within 30 days of execution of the instrument (or, if executed outside Kenya, within 30 days of its receipt in Kenya). Failure to pay is an offence, though the Government usually levies a prescribed penalty rather than prosecuting. Parties must truly declare the duty payable — a false declaration is an offence. The buyer pays stamp duty.

Who or what is exempt?

  • Transfers between associated companies.
  • Transfers to a body or registered family trust established for charitable purposes only (or its trustees).
  • Transfers between spouses.
  • Instruments under the Movable Property Security Rights Act.
  • Gifts to a charity or religious institution.
  • Transfers by the government or between government agencies.
  • Inheritance through succession.
  • First-time buyers under the Affordable Housing Scheme.

Other exemptions are found under section 117 of the Stamp Duty Act. To apply, make an application to the collector of stamp duty supported by a statutory declaration or affidavit stating the section relied upon, and attach the relevant documents.

Capital Gains Tax (CGT)

CGT is a tax imposed on the gain that accrues when a person or entity transfers, sells, or disposes of property in any manner (including by gift), whether or not for consideration. It is declared and paid by the transferor. It is the gain that is taxed, not the money received: the gain is the difference between the cost at which the property was bought and the price at which it is sold, after deducting improvement costs and incidental costs of the transfer (such as advertising and legal fees). CGT is charged at the point of transfer — on registration of the transfer instrument — at 15% of the net gain, and it is a final tax (paid once).

How to compute CGT

Net Gain = (Transfer value − incidental costs on transfer) − adjusted cost (acquisition cost + incidental costs on acquisition + any enhancement cost).

Allowable expenses include the cost of acquisition or construction, loan/mortgage interest, advertising to find a buyer, valuation costs, legal fees, and enhancement costs.

Exemptions

  • Income taxed elsewhere (e.g. property dealers).
  • A company issuing its own shares and debentures.
  • Transfer only to secure a debt or loan, and transfer by a creditor returning property used as security.
  • Transfer by a personal representative to a beneficiary during estate administration.
  • Transfers between spouses, or between former spouses in a divorce settlement or bona fide separation.
  • Transfers to immediate family, or to a company wholly owned by spouses and/or immediate family.
  • A private residence occupied continuously for the three years immediately before the transfer.
  • Internal group restructuring (group existing at least 24 months) not involving a transfer to a third party.

To pay, initiate payment on iTax, receive a payment slip, and present it at any KRA-appointed bank with the tax due.

Land rates

Land rates are a county levy on all property (freehold or leasehold) and an overriding interest. Exempt from rates are public religious worship areas; cemeteries, crematoria, and burial grounds; public health facilities; public educational institutions and libraries; wayleaves; dams; museums and national monuments; and public outdoor sports grounds.

Rates are due in the financial year levied and payable on the day appointed by the County Executive Committee member responsible for land. On full payment, the county issues a Rates Clearance Certificate. Registration of any instrument transferring or vesting an interest is accepted only when the Registrar is satisfied that all outstanding rates and county charges are paid. On default, the county may levy penalties, deny services, sue, register a charge on the property, appoint a receiver to collect rent, claim in a deceased's estate, attach debts, or auction the property. Payment is digitised — Nairobi via Nairobi Pay, and other counties via the myCounty app (rollout ongoing).

Land rent

Land rent is a levy on leasehold parcels where annual rent was reserved when the grant was issued, payable to the Ministry of Lands and Physical Planning. It is essentially payment for the right to use government-owned land for the duration of the lease, and the amount varies with location, size, and tenure. It is payable to the lessor (national or county government) every year before the end of January; the lessor may revise it, most often when the lessee seeks a development approval or lease renewal. Before any transaction on leasehold property is registered, the parties must produce a valid Rent Certificate. Land rent is not payable for freehold land.

title: Power of Attorney
excerpt: What a power of attorney is, the difference between a specific and a general POA, and how to grant and register one for land dealings in Kenya.
content:
A Power of Attorney (POA) is a formal instrument by which one person (the donor) empowers another (the donee) to represent them or act on their behalf for certain purposes. The authorisation can allow the donee to sell, purchase, manage, transfer, or lease the donor's land, take loans on it, sign transfers, and initiate litigation and legal proceedings.

You can give a specific or a general power of attorney:

  • Specific POA (also a special or limited POA) — grants authority to act for a specific purpose or for a limited time noted in the document. It is only for the action written in it.
  • General POA — open, and can be used for all or most of the donor's activities.

How to grant a power of attorney

What you need

  • Full names and addresses of the person giving the POA.
  • A passport photograph.
  • A copy of your ID.
  • A copy of your KRA PIN certificate.
  • A fee assessed at the lands registry.
  • Form LRA 5 (specific POA) or Form LRA 6 (general POA).

Where to begin

  1. Print and fill Form LRA 5 or LRA 6, stating the name of the donee and (for a specific POA) the powers granted.
  2. Sign the form before an Advocate, who also signs and stamps it — or a Notary Public if it is executed by a donor residing outside Kenya.
  3. Attach a copy of your passport photograph next to your name, and the donee's next to theirs.
  4. Pay the assessed registration fee and stamp duty at the lands registry and keep your receipt.
  5. Present the form at the registry for registration.
  6. Collect the registered power of attorney within seven working days.

Key points

  • A power of attorney lapses by operation of law — for example, on the donor's incapacity or death.
  • Before a donee can act on a matter involving immovable property, the POA must be registered in the Register of Powers of Attorney and the prescribed stamp duty paid, so the donee has the capacity to act.
  • A company can be appointed as an attorney. Where a POA is issued by a company, a copy of its Memorandum and Articles of Association and a company resolution authorising the POA must be presented.
  • Several people may appoint the same attorney jointly or separately, and several parties may join in one power appointing an attorney for their joint or separate purposes.

title: Consents & Clearances
excerpt: The written consents and clearance certificates needed before a land dealing can be registered in Kenya — from Land Control Board and spousal consent to rates and rent clearance.
content:
A consent is the written permission of the relevant authority, proprietor, manager, or interested person required under the laws affecting land registration before any dealing in a specific parcel can be lawfully registered. The specific consents and clearance certificates needed depend on where the property is situated, its tenure, and the dealing involved.

Consents

Commissioner of Lands / National Land Commission

Applies to all government leaseholds (e.g. transfers), regardless of where the property is situated. The consent is issued once the Commissioner is satisfied that all conditions, covenants, and provisions given by the Government have been complied with.

Local Land Control Board (LCB)

Required for the sale, transfer, lease, mortgage, exchange, partition, subdivision, or other dealing in agricultural land within a land control area, to ensure compliance with land-use policy and keep the land productive.

  1. Obtain and fill the LCB application forms from the District Land Registry.
  2. Attach supporting documents — a copy of the title deed, an official search, identification, passport photos, and a PIN certificate for both parties; spousal consent may be required.
  3. Submit at the Land Office and pay the prescribed non-refundable fee (application Kshs 3,000; special consent Kshs 10,000).
  4. Check the LCB meetings calendar and book a date to appear before the Board.
  5. Both parties must attend at the appointed time.
  6. The Board approves or rejects the application. If approved, you receive the consent/certificate signed by the LCB chairman.

Start early, as the process can take a few weeks. If LCB consent is not obtained, the transaction is void — even where the duty to obtain it was not exercised.

Spousal consent

Usually given as an affidavit where the other spouse seeks to charge or transfer land or a dwelling house held in their sole name.

Statutory corporations

  • Kenya Railways Corporation — for any land adjacent to railway land, KRC consent is required before any dealing.
  • Kenya Airports Authority — consent is required for properties adjoining flight paths.

These are in addition to LCB consent where applicable.

Mortgagee or chargee

Often expressly stated in the charge or mortgage document to protect the lender; it applies, for instance, when applying for a further or second charge over the property.

Landlord / head lessor

Where one holds a leasehold from Government (the head lessor) and wishes to sub-lease, the landlord's consent is needed — tenants must obtain the landlord's consent to assign or sublet.

Trustees of National Parks

Properties adjoining or within parks require this consent before any conveyancing transaction; the Kenya Wildlife Service is the trustee.

Management company

In developments with individually owned units (apartments, office suites, townhouses), the management company or corporation must approve a charge, lease, or sale of a unit.

Cautioner, registered proprietor and co-owners

  • Cautioner — once a caution is registered, any disposition inconsistent with it cannot be registered without the cautioner's consent.
  • Registered proprietor — the Registrar cannot alter the register or an instrument affecting the proprietor's title without consent, unless the proprietor caused or substantially contributed to the error through fraud or lack of proper care.
  • Tenant in common — cannot deal with their undivided share in favour of a third party (except another co-tenant) without the written consent of the others, which must not be unreasonably withheld; the Registrar may waive this where consent cannot be obtained or is unreasonably refused, recording the reasons.
  • The lender — where an undivided share or a lease held by tenants in common is charged, no partition is registered without the lender's written consent; if the lender consents, the borrower's portion remains subject to the charge while the others are discharged.
  • Occupier — a person authorised by the NLC to enter land to assess value for compulsory acquisition must obtain the occupier's consent before entering.

Clearances

Rates Clearance Certificate

Issued by the county government, confirming payment of all dues including land rates, interest, and water bills. It is a prerequisite for registering transfers. Under section 38(1) of the Land Registration Act 2012, the Registrar shall not register a transfer unless a written statement by the relevant agency certifies that all outstanding rates and charges have been paid.

Land Rent Clearance Certificate

Verifies the payment, or non-owing, of annual rent; obtaining it is mandatory before registering any transaction involving leasehold land. Under section 39(1) of the Land Registration Act 2012, the Registrar shall not register an instrument transferring or creating an interest in land unless a certificate confirms that no rent is owing to the national or county government (see also sections 55 and 56(4)).

title: Transmission of Land
excerpt: How land passes by operation of law — on death, bankruptcy, or a company's liquidation — including succession requirements and how the registry transmits title to a personal representative.
content:
Transmissions are transfers where an interest in land, a lease, or a charge passes from one person to another by an act or operation of the law — for example when someone dies or is declared bankrupt. It also includes compulsory acquisition. The form is either an assent or a transfer of interest in an estate by an administrator. Succession applications facilitate the legal transfer of land from a deceased person to their rightful beneficiaries, as specified in a will or through a grant of letters of administration.

Requirements

  • Form LRA 39 or 42.
  • Letters of administration or confirmation of grant.
  • Proof of stamp duty.
  • The original title.
  • ID/passport, PIN certificate, and two passport-size photos.

Death of a sole proprietor or proprietor in common

A sole proprietor owns land alone, while proprietors in common own shares of the parcel (equal or varying). To transfer such land after death, a Confirmation of Grant is required. The applicant applies to court for a Grant of Probate (where the owner left a will naming an executor) or a Grant of Letters of Administration Intestate (where there is no will). If the application is allowed, the executor and/or administrator (the personal representatives) are granted a Confirmation of Grant.

On being provided a copy of the Confirmation of Grant, the Land Registrar registers the person named in the grant as the owner. The Registrar may then register, by transmission, any subsequent transfer, surrender of lease, or discharge of charge by the personal representative, without requiring the personal representative to be registered. The fee to register the beneficiary named in the grant is KES 1,000. Where there is more than one proprietor, the person named in the grant becomes owner of the inherited share. Registration of the personal representative takes effect from the date of death of the proprietor.

Death of a joint proprietor

Joint proprietors own all the shares of the parcel together (for example, land owned by spouses). When one dies, the survivor automatically inherits the whole parcel. The survivor submits a death certificate to the Land Registrar and, on payment of Kshs 500, the Registrar deletes the deceased's name from the register, giving the survivor rights to the whole parcel.

Bankruptcy

Once a person is adjudged bankrupt and a Bankruptcy Order is issued, the property automatically vests in the bankruptcy trustee (or the Official Receiver if there is no trustee), who is entitled to recover assets transferred within the two years immediately preceding the bankruptcy. The trustee arranges for the transmission of the interest to be registered, or gives notice to the mortgagee or chargee that they cannot or do not intend to register it. That notice confirms the interest has vested in the trustee, and makes the mortgagee or chargee, on taking possession or selling, liable to account to the trustee as if the trustee were the proprietor.

Company liquidation

A company may be liquidated voluntarily or by the court.

Voluntary liquidation

  • By directors — the directors (or a majority) elect to liquidate; 14 days after the resolution, the company lodges a copy of the declaration with the Registrar.
  • By members — the company in general meeting appoints one or more liquidators to wind up its affairs and distribute its assets.
  • By creditors — creditors and the company appoint an insolvency practitioner to do the same.

After appointment, the insolvency practitioner may dispose of the property by transmission. Unless the articles provide otherwise, the property is distributed to members according to their interests and rights in the company.

Liquidation by the court

Only the High Court may order this, where: (a) the company resolves by special resolution to be wound up by the court; (b) a public company has not obtained a trading certificate within 12 months of registration; (c) it fails to commence business within 12 months or suspends business for a full year; (d) (except private companies) its membership falls below two; (e) it is unable to pay its debts; (f) a moratorium ends without a voluntary arrangement taking effect; (g) the court considers it just and equitable; (h) the Attorney-General applies on public-interest grounds; or (i) the Official Receiver applies. If a liquidation order is made, within 7 days the company lodges a copy with the Official Receiver and the Registrar. On the order and the appointment of a liquidator, the liquidator assumes control of the company's property (transmission).

Other cases

Where a person becomes entitled to land, a lease, or a charge under any law, or through a court order or certificate of sale, the Registrar shall, on application by an interested party and on being satisfied with the evidence, register that person as the proprietor.

title: Leases & Licences
excerpt: The essentials of leases in Kenya — registration, the difference between lease extension and renewal, and how leases are terminated — and how a licence differs from a lease.
content:
Leases

A lease is an interest in land for a specific period, subject to payment of rent and to conditions imposed by the lessor (landlord) on the lessee (tenant). In Kenya the government grants leases, especially in urban areas, to safeguard community interests and keep direct control of land use and development. The National Land Policy recommends leases of not more than 99 years, and such leases were converted to 99 years with effect from 1 September 2010 after the promulgation of the 2010 Constitution.

Registration of leases

  • Leases of more than 2 years should be registered.
  • After a lease requiring the lessor's consent is registered, no dealing is registered without that consent.
  • No Certificate of Lease is issued unless the lease exceeds 21 years.
  • Unregistered instruments are construed as contracts.

Extension versus renewal

Extension is a continuation of the same lease (time added). It is granted by the government through the National Land Commission (NLC) when the lessee applies before the existing term expires, using Form LRA 22. An extension preserves the priority of interests (such as charges or cautions) and avoids the risk of the land reverting to the lessor.

Renewal is the grant of a new lease after the old one has expired, using Form LA 23. Because the term has expired, the land reverts to the lessor (national or county government), who re-allocates to the lessee if they meet all the conditions of the previous lease and the land is not required for a public purpose. The new term runs from the date of expiry of the old term.

Risks of renewal

It is advisable to apply for an extension rather than a renewal. The NLC usually notifies the lessee about 5 years before expiry, because on a renewal:

  • Previous interests do not automatically continue (e.g. a bank charge over the old lease does not automatically attach to the new one).
  • A caution or inhibition must be re-registered.
  • Beneficial interests may be lost if not protected.

Process of renewal or extension

  1. Lodge an application at the relevant County Government office where the land is located.
  2. The County Land Management Boards (CLMB) of the NLC consider it, with input from the sections dealing with public health, roads, rates, water, and sewerage.
  3. The national Survey and Physical Planning departments are also consulted before the CLMB grants approval.
  4. The NLC prepares a new lease bearing the extended term and an enhanced annual rent after re-valuation by a government valuer (approval fee KES 5,000, paid by the lessee).
  5. On an extension, the lessee surrenders the existing title and, on paying the legal fees, a new lease/title is prepared. On a renewal, a letter of allotment is issued and, on payment, a new lease/title is prepared. The new lease is registered by the relevant Land Registry.

Termination of leases

  • Effluxion of time — expiry of the term stated in the lease.
  • Notice — must be provided for in the lease, stating the notice period; not necessary for fixed-period leases.
  • Forfeiture — where the lessee breaches covenants, is adjudged bankrupt, or goes into liquidation; it may be court-assisted. If the lessor does not act on a breach, the right of forfeiture is waived, so action must be taken within a reasonable time of detecting the breach.
  • Surrender — the lessee yields up their interest to the lessor, usually by mutual consent; without consent, the lessor may claim rent for the unexpired term by civil suit.
  • Merger — of the leasehold and reversionary interests, which must vest in the same person.
  • Frustration — destruction of the property by fire, earthquake, civil commotion, etc. entitles the lessee to terminate if it has not been repaired after 6 months, by giving 1 month's notice.

Licences

A licensee is granted a right to enter or use premises without becoming entitled to exclusive possession — for example a kiosk or vehicle parking. A licence cannot be assigned to a third party: you cannot mortgage, transfer, or inherit it. It is permission by the proprietor for the licensee to do an act on the land that would otherwise be trespass, but it does not include an easement or profit. Licences may arise expressly (in writing or orally) or impliedly from the parties' conduct, and in commercial settings are often used to allow occupation without creating a controlled tenancy or leasehold.

Licences between private persons

  • Do not create an interest in land and are therefore generally not registrable.
  • Do not confer exclusive possession, which distinguishes them from a lease or tenancy.
  • Are typically revocable at will, unless supported by contractual terms.

Licences from Government (through the NLC)

The NLC can grant a licence over unalienated land subject to planning principles and regulatory conditions. The period is limited to a maximum of five years, and the NLC's power to issue a notice to quit after nine months shows the precarious nature of a licence and the State's continuing control over public land. The licensee may, with the Commission's consent, transfer the benefit of a licence, with the transfer and consent endorsed on it. The NLC may declare a licence forfeited if the licence fee is unpaid for one month after becoming due; any tax on the land, a structure on it, or the licence remains unpaid for two months after becoming due; or the occupant fails to abide by the conditions of the licence.

title: Land Subdivision & Survey
excerpt: How land is subdivided into separate titles in Kenya — why owners subdivide, the documents and step-by-step process, the properties that cannot be subdivided, and what a mutation and a deed plan are.
content:
Subdivision is the division of land into two or more parcels, creating multiple distinct titles for individual portions. It is provided for under the Physical Planning Act, Cap 286, and specifically under section 41 of that Act.

Why subdivide?

  • Inheritance — so each beneficiary receives a defined portion.
  • Profit — smaller parcels are easier to sell and may attract a higher cumulative value, helping owners raise funds.
  • Development — part of the land may be sold to finance construction on the remaining portion.
  • Gifting — to allocate portions to individuals or institutions such as churches or schools.
  • Optimisation and planning — to optimise land use, comply with zoning, and tailor land to current needs while enhancing value (e.g. converting a large agricultural parcel into residential plots).

Required documents

  • Original title deed.
  • An official search.
  • PPA1 form.
  • Four copies of a subdivision scheme plan signed by the Physical Planner.
  • Proof of payment of fees and taxes, if any.
  • A map showing where the land is situated (Registry Index Map / Survey Map).
  • LCB consent.
  • Land Rates Clearance Certificate.

The process

  1. Conduct an official search to verify the title and the registered owner.
  2. Engage a licensed surveyor to obtain the Registry Index Map showing the land's borders.
  3. The surveyor takes measurements and creates a subdivision scheme plan, signed by a registered physical planner who issues the PPA1 form.
  4. Submit the application to the County Government via the PPA1 form.
  5. The plans are circulated to relevant government offices for comments, and to the Land Control Board if agricultural land is affected (obtain LCB consent for agricultural land, or spousal consent for matrimonial land).
  6. The county verifies and, if satisfied, issues a PPA2 (if rejected with comments, you appeal to the Liaison Committee).
  7. Submit the approved scheme to a registered surveyor for survey.
  8. A government surveyor approves the survey, verifies its accuracy, and provides fresh title numbers.
  9. The surveyor registers the new titles with the County Land Registry.

Properties that cannot be subdivided

  • A property that is collateral for a loan in a financial institution.
  • A property with a caveat on it.
  • A property with a pending court case.

Can you search land during subdivision?

The land search is closed during subdivision because of the frequent file movement in the registry, and you may not find the green card for the sub-titles until the process is complete and all green cards are returned. When buying land under subdivision at the concept level, you can only search the original title deed, not the sub-titles.

What is a mutation?

The mutation form shows how a larger (mother) parcel mutated into smaller pieces, with the proprietor's details (names, ID, box number, signature) and the date of survey. It details the subdivision (existing roads, the LR numbers of the resultant plots, and their exact measurements and areas in hectares), and is signed by a licensed/district surveyor and the land registrar. It is forwarded to Survey of Kenya to amend the Registry Index Map (RIM), which tracks all subdivisions in an area.

What is a deed plan?

A deed plan is a plan signed by the Director of Surveys showing the precise particulars of a surveyed parcel: the shape of the plot, the distances and bearings around it, the scale, the deed plan number, the land reference number, the size in hectares, the Director's signature and date of authentication, and whether the plot is a new grant or an extension of lease. Once prepared, it is attached to a certificate defining the current owner and any endorsements by the Registrar.

title: Prescription / Adverse Possession
excerpt: How occupying land openly for 12 years can ripen into ownership, who can claim adverse possession, the defences against it, the court process, and how owners can protect themselves.
content:
Adverse possession enables a person who has occupied land continuously for 12 years, without interruption or opposition from the registered owner, to claim ownership rights and gain title. A claimant must prove non-permissive, actual, open, notorious, exclusive, and adverse occupation of the land for an uninterrupted period of 12 years.

Section 38(1) of the Limitation of Actions Act, Cap 22 allows a person entitled by adverse possession to land (or a lease) registered under the Acts cited in section 37 to apply to the High Court to be registered as proprietor in place of the registered owner. Section 7 provides that an action to recover land may not be brought after 12 years from the date the right of action accrued.

Who can make a claim?

  • A squatter, caretaker, or informal occupant.
  • A licensee or tenant whose term has expired — not during a subsisting tenancy or licence, unless they continue to occupy after expiry without consent.
  • A neighbour who encroaches over a boundary, provided all the legal requirements are met.
  • Family members under unwritten licences or informal arrangements that start permissively but are never revoked or formalised.

Defences against adverse possession

  • Legal action was taken to recover the land before the 12 years elapsed.
  • The occupier was on the land with permission (e.g. as a tenant or licensee).
  • The occupation was not exclusive or was interrupted — the 12-year period may reset if the owner files suit, takes possession, or issues an eviction notice.
  • The occupation was not open or was conducted in secrecy.
  • The land belongs to the government or is held in trust by county governments.
  • A person in joint possession with the owner cannot claim unless they oust or exclude the co-owner.

How to invoke the doctrine

It is a court process, and the possessor must prove open, continuous, uninterrupted occupation for 12 years.

  1. File a suit in the Environment and Land Court (ELC) under Order 37 Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Rules, 2010, including a supporting affidavit of the facts of possession, a copy of the extract of title, and evidence of continuous occupation for at least 12 years.
  2. The respondent (usually the registered owner) must be notified and allowed to contest the claim.
  3. Once satisfied the statutory period has lapsed and all elements are proved, the court may order the applicant registered as the new owner, and the previous title is extinguished.

A person cannot claim adverse possession while simultaneously disputing the validity of the registered title.

How owners can protect themselves

  • Take actual physical possession of the land upon completion.
  • Demand vacant possession at handover and document it through signed possession certificates and dated photographs.
  • Enforce leases, re-entry, and court-ordered eviction where a tenant overstays, a licence is terminated but the occupant remains, or the occupier stops paying rent.
  • Initiate eviction proceedings against long-standing tenants who stop paying rent but continue to occupy.
  • Formalise intra-family land use through revocable tenancies, licences, declarations, and succession structures.

title: Loss of Land Documents & Reconstruction of the Register
excerpt: What to do when a title or the land register is lost or destroyed — replacing a lost title with Form LRA 12 and the 60-day gazette notice, and reconstructing the register with Forms LRA 14 to 18.
content:
Where a title to land or a certificate of lease is lost or destroyed, the proprietor may apply to the Registrar for a duplicate, producing evidence to convince the Registrar of the loss or destruction. The Registrar also has power to reconstruct a lost or destroyed land register, after appropriate inquiries and a 60-day notice in the gazette.

Loss of a title document

Requirements

  • Police abstract.
  • Statutory declaration.
  • Newspaper and Kenya Gazette notice (advertisement fee payable).
  • ID/passport, PIN certificate, two passport-size photos.
  • Application (statutory fee of KES 1,000).
  • Indemnity form.

How to apply for a replacement

  1. Report the loss or destruction to the nearest police station and obtain an abstract, presenting a copy of the title (or the title number) and your original ID/passport.
  2. Conduct an official search to prove legal ownership of the property.
  3. Make a sworn statutory declaration explaining the circumstances of the loss (for a company, made by a director).
  4. Fill Form LRA 12 (Application for Replacement Certificate of Title/Lease on Loss/Destruction).
  5. The Registrar verifies the loss, then publishes the proprietor's name in the Kenya Gazette via Form LRA 13 and in at least two national dailies, to prevent fraud or competing claims, giving 60 days' notice.
  6. The Registrar issues a provisional certificate on the expiry of 60 days from the date of publication.

If a lost title is later found, it must be delivered to the Registrar for cancellation.

Reconstruction of the land register

Where a land register is lost or destroyed, a person claiming to be the registered proprietor may apply for reconstruction using Form LRA 14, accompanied by a statutory declaration in Form LRA 15 (for a body corporate) or LRA 16 (for a natural person), and an indemnity in Form LRA 17. The Registrar publishes a notice of the loss in the Kenya Gazette using Form LRA 18, then verifies the parcel's status with the relevant authorities, including survey and land-administration offices. If no objections are raised and the information is confirmed, the Registrar may reconstruct the register.

The same procedure and Forms LRA 14–18 apply whether the problem lies on the registry's side (the register itself is lost or destroyed) or on the proprietor's side (the title documents are missing), because in both cases the Registrar must re-establish an accurate and reliable land record.

Where title was never issued

Where a title has never been issued — for instance in a succession — one may use a search certificate, a letter of allotment, or any document indicating the deceased's proprietary rights. These should be appropriately certified and/or sealed by the issuing authority to be accepted by the court. Where the title is lost, the registrar prepares an instrument for publication in the Kenya Gazette, informing the public and giving them a chance to raise objections.

title: Transfers Through Vesting Orders
excerpt: How a court vesting order transfers property without a conventional conveyance — when it is used, who and what it applies to, the requirements, and how it is registered.
content:
Vesting orders are court orders or directives that transfer ownership of property without the need for a traditional conveyance process. They are used where a normal transfer is impossible, impractical, or obstructed.

When they are issued

  • To complete a real-property transaction where a party refuses to meet its legal obligations.
  • To resolve litigation over legal or equitable interests in the family-law context.
  • On the sale of real property by companies subject to insolvency proceedings.
  • Where a transfer would otherwise be subject to subdivision, but a party has refused to cooperate.
  • Where the court sells the property in execution of a decree or orders specific performance.
  • Where the court deems it appropriate to vest property rights directly in a person or entity (e.g. property acquired through auction).

They also apply where a trustee has been appointed and that trustee is under a disability (e.g. incapacitated), is outside the jurisdiction, cannot be found, or is a dissolved corporation; where there is uncertainty as to the surviving trustees, whether a trustee is alive or dead, or who the personal representative is; or where a trustee refuses or neglects to convey land after 28 days of being required to.

How it works

A vesting order operates to vest the interest in the same manner as if it were a transfer or conveyance executed by the owner — except that here it is executed by the court. (The court is also at liberty to appoint a person to execute the conveyance instead of issuing a vesting order.)

Requirements

  • Court order.
  • Valuation report.
  • Proof of stamp duty payment.
  • ID/passport, PIN certificate, two passport-size photos.
  • The appropriate application fee.

The person acquiring the interest prepares a vesting order and sends it to court for approval and execution by a High Court judge. A vesting order is a transfer and attracts stamp duty. By registering it, the new ownership is formally recognised in the land records, ensuring the legal validity of the transfer and providing a clear, enforceable record of the change in title.

title: Allocation of Public Land
excerpt: How public land is lawfully allocated in Kenya — the NLC's six methods, the land-alienation process to acquire title, the conditions attached, and the difference between illegal and double allocation.
content:
Allocation of public land is the legal process by which the government or its agencies grant rights to public land to an individual or business enterprise. Before public land can be allocated, it must first be planned, surveyed, and serviced.

Methods of allocating public land (s.12(1), Land Act 2012)

The National Land Commission (NLC) allocates public land on behalf of the national or county governments using any of these methods:

  • Public auction to the highest bidder at the prevailing market value, not less than the reserved price. On the fall of the hammer, the agent issues a signed Certificate of Sale (Form LA 4) to the bidder and the NLC; the bidder presents it to the NLC to obtain a letter of allotment.
  • Direct allocation to specially targeted disadvantaged groups (e.g. internally displaced persons or marginalised communities). Government prepares a report on the group's status, and once the NLC is satisfied, it reserves the land for that group.
  • Public notice of tenders — the NLC invites bids at county, sub-county, and ward offices and in two dailies; bidders present bids; the NLC selects the winning bid and issues a Letter of Allotment (Form LA 5).
  • Public drawing of lots — the NLC invites applications, shortlists, and prepares lots; balloting is conducted in public; the successful applicant receives a certificate (Form LA 8) and a Letter of Allotment.
  • Public request for proposals — the NLC invites proposals for use or development, determines viable ones, and reports to the relevant government, which recommends successful applicants; the NLC issues Letters of Allotment (Form LA 5).
  • Public exchange of equal value — the NLC enters an agreement to exchange private land for public land of equal value, executes a deed of exchange or transfer, and facilitates issuance of titles (conveyance fees borne by the benefiting institution). The government cannot take possession until title has been issued to the proprietor of the exchanged land.

Acquiring title after allocation (the land-alienation process)

Before public land is allocated, plots must be hived off the public land bank:

  1. The Director of Physical Planning prepares a plan creating plots for various users.
  2. The Director of Surveys (or a private surveyor) surveys the land and numbers the parcels.
  3. The Director of Physical Planning, with the NLC and other agencies, prepares development guidelines for the area.
  4. The NLC advertises the plots, or vets targeted allottees in special cases, and oversees a fair allocation.
  5. The NLC issues letters of allotment to qualified allottees. Write to the NLC accepting the offer and its conditions, pay the statutory fees, obtain a receipt, and ensure your plot file is opened (note the number). Payment must be made within 90 days of the letter of allotment.
  6. Instruct a registered surveyor (giving them the letter of allotment, map, special conditions, and receipt) to survey your plot, show the beacons, sign a beacon certificate, and forward the survey details to the NLC.
  7. The NLC prepares and executes the lease documents on behalf of the government; the lease (Form LA 13) is forwarded to the district Chief Land Registrar for registration and issuance of the certificate of lease to the allottee.

Conditions to note

  • Most allocations carry stringent conditions which, if not complied with in time, automatically revoke the letter of allotment.
  • Wrong use of the land or non-payment of land rent and rates leads to a penalty, and the land reverts to the government for re-allocation.
  • If you cannot develop the land, surrender it so a ready allottee can be identified.
  • Allottees hold the land on a leasehold basis — the government is the lessor and the allottee the lessee.
  • The allottee must first acquire a title before transferring; a transfer on only a letter of allotment is not approved, and transfer of undeveloped allocated land is not allowed.
  • To carry out a search, the land must have a title — an unregistered letter of allotment is not recognised. A historical search may be done on the general, zone, and correspondence files, looking for planning by the local authority and the Part Development File (PDF) signed by the Chief Physical Planner and the Commissioner of Lands.

Illegal versus double allocation

An illegal allocation occurs where a party is allocated land that is not available for allocation. A double allocation occurs where the same un-alienated land is allotted to two different parties. Where a double allocation occurs and both allotments appear regular and procedural (no fraud, save for the mistake), the first in time prevails.

title: Inhibition, Caution & Restriction
excerpt: How to protect an unregistered interest in land by registering an inhibition, a caution, or a restriction against the title — what each is, how to lodge it, and how it is removed.
content:
People holding an unregistered interest in property can protect themselves by registering restrictions against the title. These are encumbrances, as they restrain the registered proprietor's right to convey any interest in the land against which they are registered.

Inhibition

An inhibition is a court process where you ask the court for orders that prevent or stop intended or current activities by others that affect your land ownership or use. It inhibits for a particular time, until a particular event occurs, or generally until a further order.

Applying for an inhibition order

  1. Prepare a document asking the court to issue the order.
  2. Swear a supporting affidavit showing why you need it.
  3. File the document at the relevant court registry, pay the assessed fee, and keep your receipt.
  4. The court assigns a case number and a hearing date.
  5. Appear in court to be heard; the respondent also presents their case.
  6. The court weighs both cases and may or may not grant the order.

An inhibition does not bind or affect the land, lease, or charge until it is formally registered — registration gives it legal effect and ensures interested parties are aware of it. Until then, the proprietor may continue to deal with the property, so register it once the court grants it.

Registering the order

  1. Fill Form LRA 66 and have it stamped by an Advocate or Court Magistrate.
  2. Attach your passport photograph and the inhibition order.
  3. Present the form at the lands registry — it is registered within seven working days.

An inhibition is cancelled on expiry of the time stated; on proof to the Registrar of a stated event occurring; on the land, lease, or charge being sold by a chargee (unless that sale is itself inhibited); or by a consequent court order.

Caution

A caution is a document lodged at the Lands Registry by someone who may have a right over land, demanding that no dealings are registered until that person has been informed. In effect, you ask the Registrar to stop other people's activities on your land.

How to place a caution

You will need a passport photograph, your ID, your KRA PIN certificate, the fee assessed by the Registrar, and Form LRA 67.

  1. Fill Form LRA 67, stating why you want the caution and how you use or own the land.
  2. Support the request with a sworn statutory declaration, stamped by an Advocate or Magistrate.
  3. Attach a copy of your ID and KRA PIN certificate.
  4. Pay the assessed fee and keep your receipt.
  5. Present the caution form at the registry.

Effects of a caution

  • The Registrar sends a notice to the persons affected by the caution.
  • It restricts the registration of dispositions and entries affecting the land, lease, or charge.
  • Any transaction prohibited by the caution is not registered.

Removing a caution

To remove a caution registered by another person, apply for its withdrawal through Form LRA 70. A Registrar may hold a hearing and make an order on whether to lift it (Form LRA 74). If the Registrar does not remove it, apply to court — a formal application supported by an affidavit, with the assessed fee paid; attend the hearing, where the respondent (who registered the caution) also presents their case, and the court may or may not grant the order. To register a court order removing a caution, fill Form LRA 70 with your reasons, support it with a verification certificate (from an Advocate, Magistrate, or Kadhi), attach a passport photograph, pay the fee, and present it. If there is an objection, the Registrar hears the parties (Form LRA 74); otherwise the caution is removed.

Withdrawing your own caution

Where you lodged a caution and now wish to remove it, fill Form LRA 69 and follow the removal steps. Note that a caution is limited to actions by the registered owner only, so routinely search the title to ensure your caution remains in place.

Restriction

A restriction asks the Lands Registrar to stop others conducting activities on your land. The Registrar may also impose one without your request where it is needed to prevent fraud or other illegal activity.

How to restrict your land

You will need a passport photograph, the fee assessed by the Registrar, and Form LRA 75. Fill Form LRA 75 stating why you want the restriction and how you use or own the land, then follow the steps for lodging a caution.
